caption: Rice root aphids living on the roots of aeroponically grown Cannabis sativa (Figure 2).
creator: Whitney Cranshaw and Suzanne Wainwright-Evans; figure photographer not separately stated in the caption
confirmation: Published Cannabis host figure in a peer-reviewed open-access article identifying Rhopalosiphum rufiabdominale on Cannabis roots.
limitations: Use as organism/root-zone reference evidence. Do not infer that generalized canopy decline uniquely identifies rice root aphid. Do not mark training-eligible until source-group and panel-level review are complete.

caption: Infection of greenhouse grown cannabis plants by Fusarium species (Figure 4), including yellowing, crown infection/decay, pith necrosis, crown rot, diseased cuttings, flower infection, cultures, and pathogenicity-test symptoms.
creator: Zamir Punja (photographs), published in Gwinn et al. 2022
confirmation: Peer-reviewed Cannabis Fusarium composite tied to published organism identification and pathogenicity evidence in the source review and cited primary studies.
limitations: Multi-panel, multi-species disease composite. Use only as a reviewed reference figure; the full composite is not a single-class training image and cannot visually confirm a Fusarium species in an unknown user plant.

caption: Cannabis plants of the Congo Durban variety infested with Phorodon cannabis, plus adult and winged adult aphids under a stereo microscope at 20× magnification (Figure 2).
creator: Daniel Lopez Restrepo and Igor Kovalchuk
confirmation: Peer-reviewed open-access Cannabis aphid study established colonies on Cannabis sativa and used morphology under 20× stereo microscopy to distinguish Phorodon cannabis from similar aphids.
limitations: Multi-panel plant-and-organism figure. Use as Cannabis host and aphid morphology reference; do not infer that yellowing or wilting alone identifies cannabis aphid. Keep training-ineligible until panel-level source grouping and crop review are complete.

caption: Cannabis powdery mildew resistance experiment showing a susceptible phenotype with dense mycelial growth beside a resistant phenotype without visible powdery mildew colonies (Figure 2).
creator: Paul D. Mihalyov and Andrea R. Garfinkel
confirmation: Peer-reviewed Cannabis powdery mildew study; the source also characterized Golovinomyces ambrosiae conidia and conidiophores from infected Cannabis leaves and used controlled inoculation/phenotyping.
limitations: Reference figure includes susceptible and resistant phenotypes under imposed disease pressure. Visible white mycelium supports powdery-mildew suspicion but does not replace organism/pathology confirmation when the causal species matters.

caption: Hemp 'Wife' plants 14 days after inoculation with pathogenic Pythium myriotylum, Globisporangium irregulare, or Fusarium oxysporum isolates, plus the uninoculated control (Figure 7).
creator: Cora S. McGehee and Rosa E. Raudales
confirmation: Controlled pathogenicity study on hemp used identified isolates, inoculation, symptom tracking, and re-isolation; Pythium myriotylum produced strong growth reduction, chlorosis, and wilt in vivo.
limitations: Multi-pathogen treatment composite. Use as controlled pathogenicity/context reference only; the whole-plant appearance is not Pythium-specific and cannot visually confirm the causal organism in an unknown plant.

caption: Cannabis stock plants and HLVd detection results from leaf and root tissues (Figure 1), with HLVd bands confirmed by sequence analysis; the study describes infected plants as showing reduced vigor, smaller leaves, stunting, and reduced inflorescence development.
creator: Zamir K. Punja, Cameron Scott, Heather H. Tso, Jack Munz, and Liam Buirs; figure photographer not separately stated
confirmation: Peer-reviewed 2025 Cannabis HLVd study using RT-PCR/RT-qPCR and sequence confirmation. Figure 1 ties sampled Cannabis plants to molecular HLVd detection rather than visual diagnosis alone.
limitations: HLVd is laboratory-bounded. Use only as a molecularly anchored Cannabis disease reference. Do not visually confirm HLVd from stunting, yellowing, small leaves, weak roots, or reduced flowering. Keep training-ineligible as a full composite.

caption: Indoor- and outdoor-grown Cannabis plants with symptoms attributed to Beet curly top virus across multiple genotypes (Figure 19); BCTV presence was confirmed by RT-PCR with universal primers.
creator: Zamir K. Punja, Dieter Kahl, Ron Reade, Yu Xiang, Jack Munz, and Punya Nachappa; visualization credited to Zamir K. Punja
confirmation: Peer-reviewed Cannabis molecular-diagnostics study. Figure 19 explicitly states that symptomatic indoor/outdoor plants were subjected to molecular diagnostics and BCTV presence was confirmed by RT-PCR.
limitations: BCTV symptoms vary by genotype and are not visually specific. Use only as a laboratory-confirmed Cannabis virus reference; do not identify BCTV from leaf curl, stunting, discoloration, or growth pattern alone. Keep training-ineligible as a full composite.
